builtins.name: download
builtins.summary: fetch a URL to a file
builtins.description: Accepts http(s) and gh://owner/repo/tag/asset, which expands to the GitHub release-asset URL. A `dest` ending in `/`, or naming an existing directory, means "into this directory under the remote filename"; anything else is the output path. The bytes stream into a temp file beside the destination and are renamed into place at the end, so an interrupted download never leaves a half-file a later run would trust. GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN, if set, is sent as a bearer token. 5xx and 429 are retried; other 4xx are not.

flags.name: --retries
flags.meaning: extra attempts after the first, with 1s/2s/4s/8s backoff

flags.name: --timeout
flags.meaning: seconds for the whole request, not per byte

flags.name: --sha256
flags.meaning: 64-character hex digest; a mismatch deletes the file and fails

builtins.name: extract
builtins.summary: unpack a zip or tar, compressed or not
builtins.description: Handles zip, tar, and .gz, .xz and .zst streams holding either a tar or a single file. The format comes from the extension, and from the leading bytes when the name says nothing. Entry names are checked before they become paths: an absolute name, or one that climbs out of `dest`, aborts the whole extraction. For a compressed single file, --member and --strip are an error, and a `dest` ending in `/` means "into this directory, under the name with the compression extension removed". Without --flatten an entry keeps the directory path it had inside the archive, so `--member sona` can land at `dest/pkg/bin/sona`.

flags.name: --member
flags.meaning: extract only this entry, matched against its full path in the archive or just its filename, so `--member chore` finds `bin/chore`

flags.name: --strip
flags.meaning: drop n leading path components from each entry; entries with fewer components are skipped

flags.name: --flatten
flags.meaning: write every entry directly into `dest` under its base name, dropping the directory path it had inside the archive; two entries that would collide is an error, and it cannot be combined with --strip

builtins.name: archive
builtins.description: The last argument is the destination, and the format comes from its extension: .zip, .tar, .tar.gz or .tgz, .tar.xz or .txz, .tar.zst or .tzst. Anything else is an error. Each source's own name is a top-level entry, as with `tar cf` and `zip -r`, so extracting gives the directory back rather than its contents loose; a source written with a trailing `/` contributes its contents instead, with no directory of its own, the way `extract` reads a trailing slash on its `dest`. Several sources pack side by side into one archive, and two of them claiming the same top-level name is an error. Entries are sorted, so the same tree packs to the same bytes twice.

builtins.name: copy
builtins.summary: copy a file or a whole directory tree
builtins.description: Missing parent directories of `dest` are created. When `dest` is an existing directory the source lands inside it under its own name, as `cp` does; otherwise `dest` is the exact path written.

builtins.name: move
builtins.summary: rename or move a file or directory
builtins.description: A rename where the filesystem allows one, a copy-then-delete across volumes. Same `dest`-is-a-directory rule as `copy`. A missing source is an error, unlike `remove`.

builtins.name: remove
builtins.description: Recursive, and silent about paths that are already gone, so a cleanup task is safe to run twice. Refuses the filesystem root and $ROOT itself; everything under $ROOT is fair game.

builtins.name: mkdir
builtins.description: Always -p: parent directories are created, and a directory that already exists is not an error.

builtins.name: chmod
builtins.description: An octal mode, with or without a leading 0 or 0o. Windows has no mode to set, so only the owner-write bit is read there: clearing it marks the file read-only, setting it clears the flag. The execute bit is ignored on Windows, where a file is executable by extension.

builtins.name: which
builtins.description: Prints the resolved path and exits 0, or prints nothing and exits 1, so `if which cargo { }` works. A name containing `/` is treated as a path rather than a PATH lookup. On Windows every PATHEXT suffix is tried, the name as written first.

builtins.name: find
builtins.summary: list matching paths under a directory
builtins.description: Every entry under `root` whose filename matches one of the patterns, one per line, depth-first and sorted. Patterns support `*` and `?` and match the filename only, case-sensitively on every platform. Results are printed with `root` as it was written, so they can be fed straight back to another command. A `root` that is not a directory is an error. Symlinked directories are not followed.

builtins.name: read
builtins.description: Contents with surrounding whitespace removed, which is what `$(...)` would do to them anyway.

builtins.name: write
builtins.description: Overwrites, creating parent directories, and adds the trailing newline that `read` trims back off. Appending is the interpreter's `>>`, so there is no flag for it.

builtins.name: sha256
builtins.description: Lowercase hex, the spelling `download --sha256` and every checksum file use.

builtins.name: exists
builtins.description: Exits 0 when the path is there and 1 when it is not, and prints nothing: it exists to be the condition of an `if`. A broken symlink still exists.

builtins.name: echo
builtins.description: Arguments joined with single spaces and one newline. What separates the arguments is word splitting at the call site, not the original spacing.

builtins.name: env
builtins.summary: read or set an environment variable
builtins.description: With one argument it prints the value, or exits 1 when the name is unset — a nonzero exit rather than an error, so `if env CI { }` works. With two it sets the variable for the rest of the run and for every process the run spawns. Reading still happens under --dry; setting does not.

builtins.name: fail
builtins.summary: stop the task with a message
builtins.description: Under `try`, or as a condition, it is just a command that exited nonzero. It has no effects, so --dry runs it and the preview stops where the real run would.

builtins.name: sleep
builtins.description: Fractional seconds are allowed. Skipped under --dry, which is meant to be instant.

variables.name: ENV
variables.meaning: the Windows toolchain; empty everywhere else

variables.name: PLATFORM
variables.meaning: the pair, for naming release artifacts

variables.name: TRIPLE
variables.meaning: the rustc target triple, for anything handed to a toolchain

variables.name: EXE
variables.meaning: the executable suffix, so `build/tool$EXE` is portable

variables.name: HOME
variables.meaning: the user's home directory, from HOME or USERPROFILE; empty if unset

variables.name: ROOT
variables.meaning: the directory holding the top-level chorefile; one per invocation, and unchanged inside included files

variables.name: CWD
variables.meaning: the interpreter's current directory. `cd` moves it, and the move dies with the task that made it, so it is per-task rather than per-run

variables.name: TASK
variables.meaning: the task currently running; a called task sees its own name, not its caller's

variables.name: NOW
variables.meaning: UTC timestamp, taken once per invocation so two lines of one recipe cannot disagree

syntax.name: assignment
syntax.meaning: Set a variable. Inside a task it is local to that task; at the top level it is a global, evaluated once before the first task runs.

syntax.name: interpolation
syntax.meaning: Substitute a variable. `$1`, `$2`, ... are a task's parameters, `$@` all of them as separate words, `$#` the count.

syntax.name: capture
syntax.meaning: Run the command and substitute its stdout with surrounding whitespace removed. A nonzero exit fails the statement unless it is wrapped in `try`.

syntax.name: if
syntax.syntax: if cond { } else if cond { } else { }
syntax.example: if $OS == windows { echo msvc } else if $OS == macos { echo apple } else { echo other }
syntax.meaning: Branch on a condition. `else if` and `else` are both optional.

syntax.name: for
syntax.meaning: Iterate. Each word is split on whitespace after interpolation, so one `$(find ...)` yields one iteration per match.

syntax.name: try
syntax.meaning: Run the command and continue even if it exits nonzero.

syntax.name: exit
syntax.meaning: Stop the run with the given code, 0 by default. A called task's `exit` unwinds its caller too.

syntax.name: return
syntax.meaning: End the current task and hand control back to its caller, which carries on. An optional code becomes the task's exit status, so `&&`, `||`, `try`, a condition and a capture read it as they read any command's. Inside a `for` it leaves the task, not the loop.

syntax.name: task
syntax.example:
# Build the release binary
task build target { cargo build --release --target $target }
syntax.meaning: Define a task. Parameters bind to `$1`, `$2`, ... in the body. The comment line directly above the `task` is its description, which `chore list` prints.

syntax.name: include
syntax.meaning: Pull another chorefile in and merge it. Paths resolve relative to the including file, a directory means the chorefile inside it, and `$ROOT` stays the top-level chorefile's directory. `as` namespaces both tasks and globals as `libs::build`; without it everything merges flat, where a duplicate name across two files is an error. A cycle names the whole loop.

conditions.meaning: string equality; compare against "" to test for empty
any command, true when it exits 0. `exists path` and `which name` are the two written for this position.

chaining.meaning: run the right side only if the left exited 0
run the right side only if the left exited nonzero
pipe the left side's stdout into the right side's stdin; the pipeline's status is the last command's
write stdout to a file, truncating it

resolution.name: task
resolution.rule: A task defined in the chorefile wins, so a project can name a task `build` and call it from another task.

resolution.name: builtin
resolution.rule: Then a builtin. Builtins are reserved: `check` reports a task that shadows one.

resolution.name: PATH
resolution.rule: Then a program on PATH, run directly — never through a shell.
A leading `^` skips straight to PATH: `^find src -name '*.rs'` runs the system find rather than the builtin.

resolution.name: cd
resolution.rule: `cd` is neither a task nor a builtin: it moves the interpreter's directory, not the process's, and the move is undone when the task that made it returns.

rules.name: word splitting
rules.rule: A quoted word is always exactly one argument. An unquoted `$var` splits on whitespace, as in sh. There are no arrays and no quoting inside a variable, so an argument that contains a space must be written quoted at the call site: `-G "MinGW Makefiles"`, not `-G $generator`.

rules.name: no shell
rules.rule: argv is handed to the OS directly. Nothing is re-quoted, re-expanded, or globbed by a shell, so shell metacharacters in an argument reach the program as literal characters.

rules.name: run once
rules.rule: A task runs once per invocation, keyed on name AND arguments, so a parameterised task called twice with different arguments runs twice. `--force` disables it.

rules.name: --dry
rules.rule: Echoes every command and skips the ones with effects, but captures and conditions still run: a `$(...)` that did not execute would leave every interpolated path downstream empty and the preview would describe a run that could never happen.

rules.name: paths
rules.rule: Paths are always written with `/`, on every platform, and converted to `\` only when handed to Windows. Paths printed back — by `find`, `which`, `$CWD`, `$ROOT` — use `/` too.

rules.name: reserved tasks
rules.rule: `list`, `help`, `check` and `spec` are subcommands, so a task may not take those names. `::` is reserved in a task name for include namespaces.

rules.name: top-level statements
rules.rule: Top-level assignments are evaluated once, before the first task. `list`, `help`, `check` and `spec` never evaluate them, so those subcommands do no I/O and work even when a file a global reads is missing.

rules.name: failure
rules.rule: Fail fast: a nonzero exit stops the task unless it is wrapped in `try` or being used as a condition. Output streams as it is produced rather than being buffered to the end.

rules.name: portability
rules.rule: `check` flags non-portable commands — curl, wget, unzip, tar, cp, mv, rm, cat, shasum, test — and names the builtin that replaces each.
